question.knowledge_point: Determining the Dimensions of the Transpose of a Matrix
question.problem:
Consider the matrix
    $L=[\begin{aligned}3 & -4 & 5 & -1 & 2 \\ -2 & -1 & 0 & -1 & 2 \\ 8 & 0 & 1 & -4 & 6\end{aligned}].$
What are the dimensions of ${L}^{T}?$
question.worked_solution:
When a matrix is transposed, its dimensions switch from $m\times n$ to $n\times m.$

So, since $L$ is a $3\times 5$ matrix, the transpose ${L}^{T}$ is a $5\times 3$ matrix.

evidence.solution_quote: So, since $L$ is a $3\times 5$ matrix, the transpose ${L}^{T}$ is a $5\times 3$ matrix.

question.knowledge_point: Finding a Scalar Factor in a Linear Combination
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14073957/assets/4b7c8c679171c1dcb6ef44b33696ba2ccce87b3f690643af979476d8dfb285ce.png)

Consider the picture above. Given that $c=\lambda a+3b$, find $\lambda .$
question.worked_solution:
To find $\lambda ,$ we want to match the expression

$$
c=\lambda a+3b.
$$

We are given that one of the components is $3b.$ So, we first draw the vector $3b$ from the origin. Then we complete the path to the point $C.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14073957/assets/f67af4512a7ab61f862932a60dafc25ef62bc46335b7d7df323fe889f8728e6b.png)

Let $P$ be the endpoint of the vector $3b.$ Then

$$
c=\overset{\to }{OP}+\overset{\to }{PC}.
$$

In $△OPC,$ we have:

- $PC=\frac{1}{2}|a|$

- $\overset{\to }{PC}$ and $a$ have the same direction

Hence, $\overset{\to }{PC}=\frac{1}{2}a.$

Additionally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}c & =\overset{\to }{OP}+\overset{\to }{PC} \\  & =3b+\frac{1}{2}a.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $c=\lambda a+3b=\frac{1}{2}a+3b.$

Since $a∦b,$ the linear combination can only be written in one way. Equating the coefficients of $a,$ we get:

$$
\lambda =\frac{1}{2}
$$

evidence.solution_quote: \lambda =\frac{1}{2}

question.problem:

Consider the picture above. Given that $l=\lambda j+\mu k$, find $\lambda $ and $\mu .$
question.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14073957/assets/6c9273c0b89d4c06c8a8591b8e8e94b0c83b2d1d4bd04b64ed8cb0a185619b5f.png)

In $△OJL$ shown above, we have 

- $OJ=|j|$

- $\overset{\to }{OJ}$ has the opposite direction to $j$

Hence, $\overset{\to }{OJ}=-j.$

Similarly:

- $JL=2|k|$

- $\overset{\to }{JL}$ has the opposite direction to $k$

Hence, $\overset{\to }{JL}=-2k.$

Additionally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}l & =\overset{\to }{OJ}+\overset{\to }{JL} \\  & =-j-2k.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $l=\lambda j+\mu k=-j-2k.$

Since $j∦k,$ the linear combination can only be written in one way. Equating the coefficients, we get:

- $\lambda =-1$ and $\mu =-2$

question.problem:
Determine which of the following second-order ODEs are homogeneous, and which are inhomogeneous.$\,$ The equation $\,\sqrt{x}\,{y}^{″}-2x{y}^{′}+y=0$ is {{field-1}}. 

$\,$ The equation $\,{y}^{″}+3{y}^{′}=x$ is {{field-2}}. 

$\,$ The equation $\,{y}^{″}-xy+4x=0$ is {{field-3}}.
question.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a second-order linear ODE given in the form

$$
a(x){y}^{″}+b(x){y}^{′}+c(x)y=f(x).
$$

The equation is homogeneous if $f(x)=0$ for all $x.$ If it is not homogeneous, then it is inhomogeneous.

With that in mind, let's examine each option.

- The equation

$$
\sqrt{x}\,{y}^{″}-2x{y}^{′}+y=0
$$

is $\text{homogeneous}$ since, for the right-hand side, we have $f(x)=0$ for all $x.$

- The equation

$$
{y}^{″}+3{y}^{′}=x
$$

is $\text{inhomogeneous}$ since, for the right-hand side, we have $f(x)=x,$ which is different from zero.

- Writing the equation

$$
{y}^{″}-xy+4x=0
$$

in the form $a{y}^{″}+b{y}^{′}+cy=f,$ we have

$$
{y}^{″}-xy=-4x.
$$

This equation is $\text{inhomogeneous}$ since, for the right-hand side, we have $f(x)=-4x,$ which is different from zero.

question.problem: For the differential equation ${x}^{2}{y}^{″}-5x{y}^{′}+8y=2x,$ what is the associated homogeneous equation?
question.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a second-order inhomogeneous ODE given in the form

$$
a(x){y}^{″}+b(x){y}^{′}+c(x)y=f(x).
$$

The associated homogeneous equation is constructed by replacing $f(x)$ with zero:

$$
a(x){y}^{″}+b(x){y}^{′}+c(x)y=0
$$

Therefore, in our case, the associated homogeneous equation is

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}-5x{y}^{′}+8y=0.
$$

question.problem:
Calculate the minor of the entry ${x}_{21}$ in the matrix
$X=[\begin{aligned}9 & -3 & 0 \\ -2 & 8 & 6 \\ -1 & 0 & 11\end{aligned}].$
question.worked_solution:
The minor of ${x}_{21}=-2$ (second row, first column) is the determinant of the remaining entries when the column and row containing $-2$ are removed: 

$$
X=[\begin{aligned}∗ & -3 & 0 \\ -2 & ∗ & ∗ \\ ∗ & 0 & 11\end{aligned}]
$$

So, the minor of ${x}_{21}=-2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 \\ 0 & 11\end{aligned}] & =|\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 \\ 0 & 11\end{aligned}| \\  & =-3\cdot 11-0\cdot 0 \\  & =-33-0 \\  & =-33.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Solving for an Unknown Given the Value of a Minor
question.problem:
Given that the minor of ${p}_{23}$ is ${t}^{2}+12$, find all the possible values of $t$ in the matrix

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}t & -8 & 3 \\ -7 & 4 & 4 \\ -1 & 9 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, we remove the second row and third column:

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}t & -8 & ∗ \\ ∗ & ∗ & 4 \\ -1 & 9 & ∗\end{aligned}]
$$

The minor of ${p}_{23}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}[\begin{aligned}t & -8 \\ -1 & 9\end{aligned}] & =|\begin{aligned}t & -8 \\ -1 & 9\end{aligned}| \\  & =t\cdot 9-(-8)\cdot (-1) \\  & =9t-8.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the minor of ${p}_{23}$ is ${t}^{2}+12$, so we must have:

$$
\begin{aligned}9t-8 & ={t}^{2}+12 \\ {t}^{2}-9t+20 & =0 \\ (t-5)(t-4) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $t=4$ and $t=5.$
